newsitem.title: CHINA: China ranks leaders by funerals it gives them.
newsitem.headline: China ranks leaders by funerals it gives them.

text.p: The three most important funerals of China's communist era -- those of Deng Xiaoping, Zhou Enlai and Mao Zedong -- reflect three very different men and the upheavals of communist rule.
When Chairman Mao Zedong died in September, 1976, one million weeping people packed Beijing's Tiananmen Square to bid farewell to the iron-willed father of China's communist revolution.

Earlier that year, when the country's beloved Premier Zhou Enlai died in the midst of a power struggle with the ultra-leftist "Gang of Four", just 5,000 people were allowed to attend the bleak official funeral ceremony.
For China's top leaders, the state funeral is an attempt to fix their place in the political pantheon, and rank is assigned through delicate calibrations of official grief and public honorifics.
Beijing's plan for Deng Xiaoping, who died on Wednesday aged 92, steers halfway between the theatrical blockbuster of Mao's funeral and the chilly send-off given to Zhou Enlai.

The official plan calls for 10,000 participants at Tuesday's ceremony in Beijing's Great Hall of the People, and the rites will be televised live to a nation where -- unlike two decades ago -- many people are now rich enough to own television sets.

While China stopped dead in its tracks for 20 days of official mourning after Mao's death, the official mourning period for Deng was set at a respectful six days, marked almost solely by flags being set at half-staff.

One key element of previous official Chinese funerals will be missing for Deng. His family respected his lifelong abhorrence of the cult of personality, ordering that his body be cremated and there be no public period of lying in state.
Mao, who also asked to be cremated, was quickly overruled by anxious leaders after his death.

Instead, some 300,000 people paid respects to his body during seven days of lying in state before the huge public memorial service. He was then embalmed for permanent display at a specially-constructed tomb in the middle of Tiananmen Square.

Zhou Enlai, too, lay in state for four days -- giving tens of thousands of people an opportunity to grieve personally over the corpse of a leader widely seen as reining in some of the excesses of the radical 1966-76 Cultural Revolution.

But radical leaders, including Mao's wife Jiang Qing, still held sway in Beijing and Zhou's official funeral ceremony was a bare-bones affair. Flags were lowered for just one day, and only 5,000 mourners were allowed to participate. The plan to downplay Zhou's funeral backfired, however. In April 1976, as China marked the traditional Qing Ming festival honouring the dead, enormous crowds gathered at Tiananmen Square to lay wreaths and read eulogies to the departed leader.

Peaceful expressions of bottled-up grief over Zhou's death quickly turned into denunciations of the Gang of Four, spurring the government to send militiamen and police into the square to clear out the "counterrevolutionary" mourners in what is now officially called the "Tiananmen Incident".

That clash, exposing the deep popular anger over the leftist nightmare China had been put through, set the stage for the removal of the Gang of Four after Mao's death on September 9 and the rise of the leader China mourns on Tuesday, Deng Xiaoping.
